newsitem.title: USA: Lead price to recover, but surpluses loom - CRU.
newsitem.headline: Lead price to recover, but surpluses loom - CRU.

text.p: The price of lead is set to recover in the second half of the year, but the Western world market will move into surplus from next year to push down prices, Neil Hawkes of consultant CRU International said.

Hawkes told the annual meeting of the U.S. Lead Industries Association that the LME three months lead price was set to bounce back over $700 per tonne in the second half of the year, but will then gradually fall to $500 to $550 per tonne by 2001 as primary metal production rises.
This compares with an average lead price of $560 a tonne between 1992 and 1996, Hawkes noted.
LME three months settled Thursday at $627.00/$627.50.
CRU expected the Western world market to end this year with a deficit of 9,000 tonnes, switching to a surplus of 12,000 tonnes next year and rising to 91,000 tonnes of excess metal by 2001.
Lead prices have fallen because of a weaker than expected winter battery making season in the northern hemisphere, record Chinese exports, and rising mine supplies.
"We have had three good years and now we are due for a downtrend in prices, but hopefully a price below $600 is a price producers can live with," Hawkes said.
At $560 per tonne, or 25 cents per pound, producers "get edgy", but cutbacks in output would probably not begin until tags plunged to 20 cents or below, Hawkes added later.
LME, producer, merchant and consumer stocks have begun to creep up again but were still just below the crucial five-week level, above which prices would start to fall.
"I don't see prices falling below $600 per tonne (LME three months) for the next couple of months, and then the battery season will start and the market will tighten once more," Hawkes said.
Chinese lead exports were expected to fall this year and preliminary data was supporting this view.

However, despite the fall in lead prices, it was not clear how much Chinese exports would decline, but they were conducting more contract business than in the past, and less of the price sensitive spot deals, Hawkes said.
"I still see the (former) Eastern Bloc (countries) remaining a big exporter for the forseeable future but volumes will steadily fall," Hawkes said.
Last year, countries formerly part of the Eastern Bloc exported about 90,000 tonnes while China's exports totaled about 210,000.

Primary production was also set to grow over the next couple of years, reversing the trend of the past decade, as more zinc mines came on stream, generating lead as a by product. Secondary lead production in the West will grow more slowly because it would be difficult to improve on the already high rates of battery recycling.
The growth in lead concentrates output could create a smelter bottleneck by the end of the century, but some of this surplus concs could be soaked up by smelters in the Eastern Bloc, Hawkes said.
Future Western lead consumption will grow at one to two percent a year, driven by batteries which now consume two-thirds of lead output, Hawkes said.
